content: Salicylic acid is a topical medication primarily used for the treatment of acne and other dermatological conditions. It is approved by the FDA for managing acne, as well as for alleviating symptoms such as itching, irritation, redness, and scaling associated with psoriasis, eczema, and seborrheic dermatitis. Common side effects include hypersensitivity reactions and salicylate toxicity. For adult patients, salicylic acid is applied topically in concentrations ranging from 0.5% to 10% for acne vulgaris. For hyperkeratotic skin disorders, it can be applied as a gel to the affected area, with occlusion at night, or as a shampoo for scalp conditions, which should be worked into a lather and rinsed. For psoriasis, concentrations of 3% to 6% are used topically. For wart removal, concentrations of 5% to 40% are applied once or twice daily for up to 12 weeks. There is limited information regarding its FDA-labeled indications, off-label uses, and dosages in pediatric patients. Similarly, there is insufficient data on contraindications, clinical trial experiences, postmarketing experiences, and drug interactions. Salicylic acid is for external use only. Contact with the eyes should be avoided, and if accidental contact occurs, the area should be rinsed thoroughly with water. It should not be used over large areas of the body without consulting a physician. If the condition worsens or does not improve with use, medical advice should be sought. Prolonged use without medical supervision is not recommended. The mechanism of action of salicylic acid involves several pathways. It exerts anti-inflammatory effects by suppressing the activity of cyclooxygenase (COX), an enzyme responsible for producing pro-inflammatory mediators like prostaglandins. Unlike traditional NSAIDs, it does not directly inhibit COX but suppresses its expression through an unclear mechanism. Salicylic acid also activates adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which may contribute to its anticancer and antidiabetic effects. It uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, altering cellular energy status and potentially influencing AMPK activity. Even in the absence of AMPK, salicylic acid demonstrates antidiabetic effects, suggesting additional unknown mechanisms. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of salicylic acid during pregnancy, labor and delivery, nursing, or in pediatric, geriatric, gender-specific, racial, renal-impaired, hepatic-impaired, or immunocompromised populations. Patients are advised to wash the affected area with soap and water, pat it dry, and apply the cream to the affected area one to four times daily or as directed by a physician. The interaction between alcohol and salicylic acid has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication. One of the brand names for salicylic acid is ALA-SEPTIC®.
